title: Outage: 'the internet is down' at the Riverside branch

objective: Applying a consistent troubleshooting methodology from problem identification through documentation
secondaryObjectives: Diagnosing network service issues: switching, routing, and address pool exhaustion

sources.cite: CompTIA Network+ (V9), exam N10-009: domains Networking concepts 23%, Network implementation 20%, Network operations 19%, Network security 14%, Network troubleshooting 24%; launched 2024-06-20
sources.note: Relevant text: troubleshooting covers 'identifying the problem, establishing a theory, testing, planning, and implementing a solution,' 'verifying functionality, and documenting findings'; network services issues include 'switching issues (STP, VLAN assignment, ACLs), routing issues (routing table and default routes)'. Objective titles 5.1 'Explain the troubleshooting methodology', 5.3 'Given a scenario, troubleshoot common issues with network services', 5.5 'Given a scenario, use the appropriate tool or protocol to solve networking issues' read in CompTIA's N10-009 objectives comparison flyer (April 2024, partners.comptia.org). Both read through summarizing fetches on 2026-11-11; the objectives PDF itself was not reachable. The course objective titles are the course seed's (2026-11-07).

sources.note: Relevant text (the objective's steps as the guide lists them): 1 'Identify the problem' (gather information, question users, identify symptoms, 'Determine if anything has changed', duplicate the problem, approach multiple problems individually); 2 'Establish a theory of probable cause' (question the obvious; top-to-bottom/bottom-to-top OSI, divide and conquer); 3 'Test the theory to determine the cause' ('If theory is not confirmed, establish a new theory or escalate'); step 4 'Establish a plan of action ...' was cut off in the preview. Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-11 (the first four steps only). Steps 5-7 (implement, verify full functionality, document) are taken from CompTIA's own page wording (see the Network+ source).

sources.cite: Cisco IOS command reference, ip route
sources.note: Relevant text: 'ip route prefix mask {address | interface} [distance] [tag tag] [permanent]'; prefix 'IP route prefix for the destination'; mask 'Prefix mask for the destination'; interface 'Network interface to use'; 'no ip route prefix mask'. Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-11. That two static default routes of equal distance share traffic is the scenario's teaching model (FLAG: not read in this source); the show output layouts are authored renderings.

sources.cite: IETF RFC 1812, Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers, 2.2.5.2
sources.note: Relevant text: 'Routers must use the most specific matching route (the longest matching network prefix) when forwarding traffic.' Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-11. Why traffic to 10.20.10.53 follows the default route once the 10.20.0.0/16 route is missing.

Relevant text: 'timed out: The server didn't respond to a request after a certain amount of time and a certain number of retries'; 'Nonexistent domain: The computer or DNS domain name doesn't exist.' Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-11. The exact nslookup and tracert output in the scenario is an authored rendering.

brief.situation: You are the network technician for Larkspur Insurance (fictional). At 08:45 the Riverside branch calls: 'the internet is down.' Branch PCs use the HQ DNS server 10.20.10.53 across a VPN tunnel on the branch router BR1; internet traffic leaves BR1 straight to the ISP. The branch uploads the day's claims to HQ at 09:45, and its card terminals use the internet. Work it with the troubleshooting methodology, from identifying the problem to documenting it.
handover: BR1: default route to the ISP 203.0.113.1; HQ (10.20.0.0/16) is reached through Tunnel1.
Changes to BR1 go through a change ticket; emergency changes can be approved by phone.
howItWorks: Run commands from the command line: type one, or pick it from the suggestions or the action list. Only this lab's commands run; there is no free shell, and each command's arguments come from its list.
Each command takes operator time: run it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The outage keeps developing on the same clock.
The map shows each host, device or service and the links between them, with a status in words. Output appears in the terminal as it happens.
When you declare the service restored, you write the incident record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: How many operator minutes each command or change takes, and when the fictional outage spreads, are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values. The claims upload runs at 09:45, 60 minutes after the call.

writeup.question: For the incident record: walk the methodology. What you identified, the theory you formed and how you tested it, what you changed and how you verified it.

parts.label: Identify and theorize
parts.criteria: Questions users (names fail, an IP works) and checks what changed (last night's route change); forms the theory that the path to the HQ DNS server is broken, not the internet.
parts.modelAnswer: Users said names failed but an address worked, which points at DNS, and the change calendar showed last night's change to BR1's routes to HQ. My theory: the route change broke the path to the HQ DNS server.

parts.label: Test
parts.criteria: Confirms with tracert (DNS traffic leaving to the ISP) and show ip route (10.2.0.0/16 instead of 10.20.0.0/16, longest match falls to the default).
parts.modelAnswer: tracert to 10.20.10.53 went to the ISP, and show ip route had 10.2.0.0/16, so 10.20.10.53 matched only the default route.

parts.label: Implement, verify, document
parts.criteria: Gets the change approved, adds the correct route and removes the typo, saves, verifies with nslookup and the users, and records the cause and a preventive measure (peer review); rejects the public-resolver workaround and a reload.
parts.modelAnswer: With an emergency change approved, I added 10.20.0.0/16 via Tunnel1, removed the typo and saved. nslookup answered and the users confirmed the intranet and payments. A public resolver would hide HQ names, and a reload would just reload the saved typo.

source.cite: Infrastructure outcome profile (docs/sims.md 9.2, 22.10), tightened to 45 minutes for this case
source.note: Fixed with time to spare before the 09:45 claims upload; the scenario's own timing.
No second fault: a public resolver left handed out, a second default route, or the branch taken offline.

noProgress.rationale: Closing while branch PCs cannot resolve HQ names leaves the branch unable to work with HQ; it is never a safe outcome.

expertPath.text: Question users: names fail, an IP works, payments work. Check the change calendar: last night's route change on BR1.
Theory: the change broke the path to the HQ DNS server. Test: nslookup times out, tracert leaves via the ISP, show ip route has 10.2.0.0/16.
Get the emergency change approved, add 10.20.0.0/16 via Tunnel1, remove the typo, save, nslookup, ask the users.
Document the typo as the cause and peer review for route changes as the lesson.

fixed.headline: Good: fixed by the method
fixed.body: Every step of the methodology did its job: what changed pointed at BR1, the test proved the typo, and the users confirmed the fix.

fixedGaps.headline: Fixed, with gaps
fixedGaps.body: Names work again. The criteria show which steps were skipped or came late.

branchOffline.headline: A guess took payments down
branchOffline.body: Testing the theory first (tracert, show ip route) shows one missing route; nothing about the internet path needed changing.

claimsMissed.headline: The outage reached the claims upload
claimsMissed.body: Asking what changed points at BR1 in two minutes. The upload needed HQ names by 09:45.

stillBroken.headline: Closed too soon
stillBroken.body: Branch PCs still could not resolve HQ names. Verify full functionality before you document.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Identify: users say names fail but an IP works; the change calendar shows last night's route change on BR1. Theory: the path to the HQ DNS server is broken. Test: nslookup times out, tracert to 10.20.10.53 leaves via the ISP, show ip route has 10.2.0.0/16 instead of 10.20.0.0/16, so the longest match is the default route. Plan: emergency change with rollback. Implement: add the right route, remove the typo, save. Verify: nslookup and the users. Document: the typo as the cause, peer review as the lesson. A public resolver or a reload are not fixes.
